strengths: The paper provides a clean and insightful reformulation of F2SA as forward-difference approximation of the hypergradient, which naturally motivates generalizing to higher-order finite-difference schemes (F2SA-p); this connection is a genuine conceptual contribution that could inspire further work.

The theoretical results are comprehensive: a matching upper bound analysis (Theorem 3.1) generalizing prior p=1,2 results to arbitrary p, a tightened Lipschitz constant for p=2 (improving prior bound by a factor of kappa), and a new Omega(epsilon^{-4}) lower bound (Theorem 4.1) via a cleaner fully-separable construction than prior works, which also fixes smoothness violations in earlier lower-bound constructions.

The near-optimality argument (matching upper and lower bounds up to log factors in the high-smoothness regime p = Omega(log(1/epsilon)/loglog(1/epsilon))) is a satisfying theoretical takeaway that clarifies the achievable rates as a function of higher-order smoothness.

The proofs are detailed and appear rigorous, using established tools (Faà di Bruno formula, Vandermonde-based finite-difference coefficient derivation, NSGD/SGD convergence lemmas) with self-contained appendices.
Practical relevance is well-argued: the paper identifies F2SA-2 as a nearly 'free' improvement over F2SA (same per-iteration cost, strictly better error order), which is empirically validated.
The experimental section, while limited, shows F2SA-2 outperforming F2SA and HVP-based baselines on a real benchmark (20 Newsgroup), lending some empirical credibility to the theoretical improvement.
weaknesses: The core technical increment beyond prior work (Chen et al. 2025, Kwon et al. 2023/2024) is somewhat incremental: replacing forward difference by higher-order finite differences is a natural and not particularly deep idea once the reformulation is noted, and much of the heavy lifting (Lipschitz continuity of higher derivatives via Faà di Bruno, NSGD/SGD convergence machinery) is inherited or closely follows techniques in Chen et al. 2025 and Kwon et al.

The complexity bound O(p*kappa^{9+2/p}*epsilon^{-4-2/p}) has extremely poor dependence on the condition number kappa (kappa^9 to kappa^11), which is not discussed or empirically validated; the paper explicitly leaves tightness of kappa dependence as an open problem, weakening the practical significance of the theoretical gains.

The requirement of high-order smoothness (Assumption 2.5, pth-order Lipschitz continuity in y) is a strong and somewhat unusual assumption; the paper does not discuss how restrictive this is for realistic machine learning bilevel problems (e.g., deep network lower levels), nor verify it holds in the experimental task.

For p >= 3, the algorithm requires solving p (or p+1) lower-level problems per iteration, which is not obviously cheaper in practice than the improved asymptotic rate suggests, and the paper's own experiments find p=2 is empirically optimal, casting doubt on the practical value of the general F2SA-p family beyond p=2, which somewhat undercuts the motivation for developing the full class of algorithms.

The experimental evaluation is very limited: only one dataset/task (learn-to-regularize on 20 Newsgroup) is used, with no experiments directly probing the higher-order smoothness regime, no verification that assumption 2.5 approximately holds, and no experiments for p>=3 results/curves shown in the main text (deferred, and ultimately deemed impractical).

There remains an unresolved gap between the upper bound and lower bound for small/moderate p (including the important case p=1), which the paper acknowledges as an open problem; thus the central open question motivating much of the practical use cases (first-order smooth problems) is not resolved.

The paper's novelty is partly overlapped with concurrent/recent work (Chen et al. 2025 JMLR, Kwon et al. 2024) already achieving O(epsilon^{-6}) and near-optimal deterministic rates; the incremental nature of extending to a family of pth-order methods, while technically sound, may be seen as a natural next step rather than a groundbreaking result.

strengths: Elegant and novel reinterpretation of F2SA as a forward-difference approximation to the hyper-gradient, which naturally motivates the higher-order finite-difference generalization (F2SA-p).

Nontrivial theoretical contribution: generalizes the Faà di Bruno-based Lipschitz analysis to arbitrary order p, yielding improved SFO complexity O~(pε^{-4-2/p}) for pth-order smooth problems, and even tightens the existing p=1 and p=2 bounds by polynomial factors in the condition number.

The Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound construction is a genuine technical fix: the paper carefully shows that prior bilevel lower-bound constructions (Dagréou et al., Kwon et al.) violate the stated smoothness assumptions, and proposes a fully separable construction that is valid and clean.
The upper and lower bounds together pin down near-optimality in a well-defined 'highly smooth' regime, providing a coherent and interesting theoretical narrative.

Careful, detailed discussion of related assumptions (stochastic Hessian, mean-squared smoothness, joint high-order smoothness) clarifies how this work differs from and improves upon prior lines of work.
The F2SA-2 special case is well-motivated as a 'free lunch' improvement over F2SA (same per-iteration cost, better error guarantee), which is a practically appealing takeaway.
weaknesses: The near-optimality claim depends on assuming p can be as large as Ω(log ε^{-1}/log log ε^{-1}), which requires smoothness of increasingly higher-order derivatives of f and g in y — a very strong and arguably unrealistic assumption for most practical lower-level losses; the practical relevance of the 'highly smooth region' result is therefore questionable.

The complexity bounds have a condition-number dependence of κ^{9+2/p}, which is quite large and not shown to be tight; the authors admit the lower bound only holds for constant κ, so the 'near-optimal' claim is considerably weakened when κ is non-constant, which is the more realistic setting.

Experimental validation is thin: only a single benchmark (20 Newsgroup learn-to-regularize) is used, p is only tested up to 5, and the paper does not test on the large-scale LLM setting that is used in the introduction to motivate the practical importance of first-order bilevel methods (ScaleBiO, SEAL). This creates a mismatch between the motivating application and the empirical evidence provided.

The paper does not report wall-clock time or computational overhead of solving p (or p+1) lower-level problems per outer iteration, which is important since higher p algorithms have proportionally higher per-iteration cost; only iteration counts are shown in Figure 1.

Baselines compared in experiments (F2SA, stocBiO, MRBO, VRBO) do not include the most recent competitive first-order bilevel methods discussed in Table 1 (e.g., the two-time-scale method of Chen et al. 2025 or the method of Kwon et al. 2024), making the empirical comparison incomplete relative to the theoretical comparison table.

Much of the technical machinery (NSGD convergence lemma from Cutkosky & Mehta, SGD lemma from Kwon et al., tensor-Lipschitz composition lemma from Luo et al., Faà di Bruno formula) is imported from existing work; the core novelty is the application/generalization of finite-difference ideas rather than fundamentally new techniques, which somewhat limits the technical originality.

The open problems section candidly notes that even for the basic p=1 case the gap between upper and lower bounds remains unresolved, indicating the central open question in this line of work is still unsettled by this paper.

The paper offers no ablation or sensitivity analysis on the finite-difference step size ν, which is a critical and potentially fragile hyperparameter in practice given that too small ν can amplify stochastic noise while too large ν increases bias.

strengths: The reinterpretation of F²SA as a forward-difference hypergradient approximation is an elegant conceptual contribution that naturally motivates the higher-order finite-difference generalization (F²SA-p), and this framing is intuitive and well-explained.

The technical execution generalizing to arbitrary order p is nontrivial, requiring a careful tensor-calculus analysis (high-dimensional Faà di Bruno formula) to bound Lipschitz constants of higher-order derivatives of the value function; the authors also obtain a strictly tighter bound for p=2 compared to prior work (Chen et al.), which is a meaningful technical improvement.

The paper complements its upper bound with a new Ω(ε⁻⁴) lower bound via a cleaner, fully separable hard-instance construction, and the authors carefully explain why existing bilevel lower-bound constructions (Dagréou et al., Kwon et al.) violate the stated smoothness assumptions—this is a useful clarifying contribution to the literature.
The near-optimality result in the highly-smooth regime (p = Ω(log ε⁻¹/log log ε⁻¹)) connecting to HVP-based method complexity is a nice unifying observation.

F²SA-2 is highlighted as a practically appealing instantiation, since it has the same per-iteration cost as F²SA but with improved theoretical guarantees and no downside even absent the extra smoothness assumption, and this is empirically validated on a standard benchmark where F²SA-2 clearly outperforms F²SA and HVP-based baselines.
Related work discussion is thorough and clearly positions the contribution relative to stochastic-Hessian, mean-squared-smoothness, and jointly-high-order-smoothness assumption papers.
weaknesses: The core acceleration mechanism relies on an additional high-order smoothness assumption (Assumption 2.5) in the lower-level variable y up to order p; for p in the 'nearly optimal' regime this requires smoothness up to order Θ(log(1/ε)), which is a very strong and somewhat artificial assumption unlikely to hold for realistic machine learning objectives.

The paper's own open-problems discussion acknowledges that the practically most relevant case, p=1 (standard first-order smoothness), still has an unresolved gap between the O(ε⁻⁶) upper bound and Ω(ε⁻⁴) lower bound—so the central open question motivating the work (closing the gap for standard first-order bilevel problems) remains open.

Experimental validation is quite limited: only a single benchmark (20 Newsgroup learn-to-regularize task) is used, and while it justifies choosing p=2 in practice, there are no experiments systematically exploring higher p (e.g., p=3,4,5) to substantiate the theoretical complexity trend O(pε⁻⁴⁻²/p), nor experiments on additional bilevel tasks (e.g., meta-learning, data reweighting) to demonstrate broader applicability.

The condition-number dependence κ^{9+2/p} is quite large and not shown to be tight; the paper does not provide lower bounds or experiments addressing whether this polynomial dependence on κ is necessary, which is listed as an open problem but leaves a notable gap in the completeness of the picture in Table 1.

The paper explicitly changes the standard gradient step to a normalized gradient step for analytical convenience (Remark 3.2), and while the authors conjecture the standard gradient step also works, this is not proven, slightly weakening the completeness of the theoretical guarantees relative to prior work (e.g., Chen et al. use standard steps).

Presentation relegates the odd-p algorithm and several key lemmas/proofs entirely to the appendix, and the main text symmetric penalty formulation (Eq. 4) has a minor typographical issue (extra closing parenthesis) that slightly hampers immediate readability.

strengths: Elegant and novel theoretical insight: reinterprets F2SA's hypergradient estimator as a first-order (forward) finite-difference approximation, which naturally motivates a generalization to higher-order finite-difference schemes (F2SA-p).

Rigorous complexity analysis: improves the SFO complexity for pth-order smooth problems from O(ε^-6) to O(ε^-4-2/p), with explicit dependence on smoothness order and condition number; also tightens prior bounds even at p=1 (by a factor of κ) and p=2 (tighter Lipschitz constant via avoiding direct third-derivative computation).

Complements the upper bound with a carefully constructed Ω(ε^-4) lower bound via reduction to single-level stochastic optimization, addressing shortcomings (e.g., violated smoothness assumptions) in prior lower-bound constructions from related works, and showing near-optimality of F2SA-p in the high-smoothness regime.

Clear and thorough positioning relative to a large body of related work (BSA, stocBiO, F2SA variants, Huang et al.'s joint-smoothness approach), with explicit discussion of assumption differences and complexity comparisons summarized in a clean table.

Provides concrete, well-motivated example applications (data hyper-cleaning, learn-to-regularize) that provably satisfy the required high-order smoothness assumption, grounding the theory in plausible use cases.

Reasonably thorough proofs in the appendix, including self-contained derivation of finite-difference coefficients (even/odd p) and detailed induction arguments for Lipschitz continuity bounds using the Faà di Bruno formula.
Includes empirical validation on both a smooth (logistic regression) and nonsmooth (MLP) bilevel problem, showing that F2SA-p variants generally outperform vanilla F2SA and other baselines.
weaknesses: Very high condition-number dependence (κ^{9+2/p}) with an acknowledged Ω(κ^9) gap versus the lower bound; the paper leaves this open, weakening the claimed near-optimality (which only holds for constant κ).

The required Assumption 2.5 (high-order smoothness in y up to order p) is quite strong and may not hold for many practical bilevel problems; the paper only gives two hyperparameter-tuning style examples that provably satisfy it, leaving broader applicability unclear.

The complexity results are stated purely in terms of SFO calls, but larger p requires solving p (or p+1) lower-level problems in parallel per outer iteration; the paper does not report wall-clock time, memory, or realistic compute cost trade-offs, which matters practically since parallelization is not free.

Experimental results are somewhat inconsistent/non-monotonic in p (e.g., F2SA-8 is not always better than F2SA-5 or F2SA-3 in Figure 1), and the paper does not offer much analysis or guidance on how to select p in practice, undermining the practical takeaway of the theory.

Experiments are limited to two problem settings (logistic regression hyperparameter tuning and a single MLP task) with a single dataset each; broader benchmarking (different tasks, dataset scales, or sensitivity analysis on p and ν) would strengthen the empirical claims.

The gap between the upper and lower bound is only closed asymptotically for p = Ω(log ε^-1/log log ε^-1); for small/practical p (including the important case p=1), a meaningful gap remains open, so the 'near-optimality' claim has limited applicability outside a specific asymptotic regime.

The normalized gradient step is introduced as a technical convenience for the analysis (Remark 3.1) without full justification that standard gradient descent achieves the same rates, leaving a minor gap between the theoretically analyzed algorithm and the more commonly used unnormalized variant.

strengths: Provides a clean and genuinely insightful reinterpretation of F2SA as a forward-difference approximation to the hyper-gradient, which naturally motivates a principled generalization to higher-order finite-difference schemes (F2SA-p).

Rigorous theoretical development: Lemma 3.1 derives explicit pth-order central/forward finite-difference coefficients for vector-valued functions with clean bounds on coefficient magnitudes; Lemma 3.2 extends the Faà di Bruno-based Lipschitz analysis of the penalty function to arbitrary order and tightens prior p=2 bounds by Chen et al. (2025b).
The paper also improves the p=1 condition-number dependence over the best known F2SA bound (Chen et al., 2025b) via a tighter inner-loop analysis.

Constructs a clean separable lower-bound instance that avoids the smoothness violations present in earlier bilevel lower-bound constructions (Dagréou et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2024a), giving a valid Ω(ε^-4) lower bound under the paper's own assumption class.

Reasonably thorough placement in the literature, including detailed discussion of related assumptions (stochastic Hessian, mean-squared smoothness, jointly high-order smoothness) and honest discussion of remaining open problems (condition-number gap, gap for small p).
Includes experiments on a real dataset (20 Newsgroups) and an MLP variant showing that increasing p tends to improve empirical convergence, which is at least qualitatively consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The headline 'near-optimality' claim only holds in an impractical regime p = Ω(log ε^{-1}/log log ε^{-1}); for any fixed, practical p (including p=1 and p=2, the only cases demonstrated experimentally) there remains a large, unresolved gap to the Ω(ε^-4) lower bound (e.g., ε^-6 vs ε^-4 for p=1), so the paper's core 'faster rates' claim is somewhat oversold relative to what is actually closed.

The condition-number dependence of the upper bound (κ^{9+2/p}) is far from the best known lower bounds (κ^{4} or κ^{5/2}, per concurrent work cited by the authors themselves), leaving an Ω(κ^9) gap that the authors explicitly acknowledge as open — this undercuts the 'near-optimal' framing of the contribution.

The lower bound (Theorem 4.1) is a fairly mechanical reduction from the existing single-level SGD lower bound (Arjevani et al., 2023) via a fully separable construction; while technically clean, it is incremental rather than a new proof technique, and it does not address the harder question of tightness for small p or in κ.

Algorithm 1/2 require solving p (or p+1) lower-level subproblems per outer iteration; although described as 'parallel', this multiplies computational/memory cost by a factor of p, and the paper does not clearly discuss this practical overhead or provide a wall-clock/compute-normalized comparison in experiments.

The high-order smoothness assumption (Assumption 2.5), requiring Lipschitz continuity of derivatives up to order p in y, is strong and somewhat exotic; the two examples offered (softmax, logistic regression) are narrow and basically hand-selected to satisfy arbitrary-order smoothness, raising questions about how broadly applicable the regime p ≥ 3 (let alone large p) actually is in practice.

The experimental evaluation is limited to one logistic-regression task and one MLP task on a single dataset, with no error bars/variance reporting, no explicit measurement of SFO complexity (the actual quantity the theory bounds), and iteration counts rather than oracle-call counts are used for comparison, which can be misleading given that F2SA-p's per-iteration cost scales with p.

The overall contribution feels somewhat incremental on top of a fast-moving line of concurrent/parallel work (Chen et al. 2025b, Kwon et al. 2024a, Ji 2025, Chen & Zhang 2025, Huang et al. 2025), several of which are cited as very recent/concurrent arXiv preprints, making it hard to assess the paper's unique positioning and durability of its claimed improvements.

Remark 3.1 admits that the normalized gradient step (a non-trivial modification from prior work) is used mainly to simplify the analysis, with standard gradient descent guarantees merely conjectured ('we believe') rather than proven, leaving a gap between the analyzed algorithm and the more standard version.

strengths: Novel and clean reinterpretation of F2SA as a forward-difference approximation to the hyper-gradient, which naturally motivates a principled generalization to higher-order finite-difference schemes (F2SA-p). This conceptual contribution is elegant and provides real insight into why F2SA has suboptimal complexity.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper derives an improved SFO complexity bound O~(p*kappa^{9+2/p} * epsilon^{-4-2/p}) for pth-order smooth bilevel problems, strictly generalizing and in some regimes tightening prior results (e.g., improving the p=1 bound by a factor of kappa, and tightening the Hessian-Lipschitz constant for p=2 compared to Chen et al. 2025b).

The paper complements the upper bound with a new, carefully constructed Omega(epsilon^{-4}) lower bound for stochastic bilevel optimization, using a fully separable construction that avoids pitfalls (violations of smoothness assumptions) present in earlier lower-bound constructions by Dagreou et al. and Kwon et al.

Near-optimality is established in the highly-smooth regime (p = Omega(log(1/eps)/loglog(1/eps))), matching HVP-based method complexities while remaining a fully first-order method -- an important practical advantage since HVPs are costly and F2SA-type approaches scale better (e.g., to 32B LLM training as cited).

Good contextualization relative to a large body of related work (BSA, stocBiO, F2SA variants, FdeHBO, Huang et al., Yang et al.), including careful discussion of differing smoothness assumptions and why this paper's assumptions are more natural/weaker in certain respects.

Theoretical results are accompanied by complete, self-contained proofs (finite-difference coefficient derivations, Faa di Bruno-based Lipschitz continuity arguments, induction-based complexity proof), which adds confidence in correctness.

Empirical validation on a real hyperparameter-tuning task (data/logistic regression with provably high-order smoothness) shows F2SA-p variants (especially p=2,3,5) outperforming F2SA and other baselines, and additional experiments on a nonsmooth MLP setting show the method still provides practical benefits outside the theoretical smoothness regime.

Honest discussion of open problems (remaining gap in epsilon dependence for small p, condition-number gap of Omega(kappa^9)) showing scholarly rigor and clear delineation of what is and isn't resolved.
weaknesses: The practical benefit of using large p is unclear beyond p=2, since higher p requires stronger smoothness assumptions (Assumption 2.5) that may not hold or be hard to verify in general nonconvex ML models (e.g., the MLP experiment is nonsmooth, yet high p still improves performance empirically, which is not explained and arguably undermines the clean narrative connecting smoothness order to speedup).

The condition number dependence of the upper bound (kappa^{9+2/p}) is very large and the paper openly acknowledges an Omega(kappa^9) gap relative to known lower bounds; this limits the practical/theoretical tightness of the main results, especially since condition numbers can be large in practice.

The overall complexity improvement, while theoretically interesting, requires p to grow with log(1/epsilon)/loglog(1/epsilon) to approach near-optimality, which practically means a very large number of finite-difference points/parallel lower-level solves, raising concerns about real-world applicability (variance in gradient estimates, numerical stability of large finite-difference coefficients, parallel compute cost).

Experimental evaluation is somewhat limited in scope: only two relatively small-scale tasks (logistic regression hyperparameter tuning and a small MLP) are tested; no large-scale or LLM-related experiments are included despite the motivation drawing on LLM-scale bilevel optimization (ScaleBiO) in the introduction.

The paper does not empirically validate the theoretical epsilon-dependent rates directly (e.g., log-log plots of complexity vs. epsilon), relying instead on loss/accuracy curves vs. iterations, which do not clearly demonstrate the claimed complexity improvements empirically.

No wall-clock time or total oracle-call based comparison is provided; since F2SA-p methods require solving p (or p+1) lower-level problems per outer iteration (in parallel), it's unclear whether the per-iteration overhead negates gains in outer-loop iteration count in realistic compute-constrained settings.

The numerical stability of higher-order finite-difference coefficients (which can involve increasingly large/small combinatorial factors for larger p, as seen in the proof of Lemma 3.1) is not discussed, which is a classical concern in numerical finite-difference methods and could affect variance/practical convergence for large p.

Minor presentation issue: due to space constraints, the main paper only presents Algorithm 1 for even p, deferring the odd-p version to the appendix, making the main text slightly incomplete without consulting supplementary material.
